First AI IPO
Anthropic
filed for its IPO
yesterday, with reports suggesting it could raise up to $100B at around a $2T valuation
,
rivaling SpaceX's $2.1T record. The maker of AI chatbot Claude is reportedly planning to debut on Nasdaq the week of Nov. 16.
Anthropic earned $16.3B in revenue for the first half of 2026, a 1,304% increase from the year before. However, filings reveal it relies on two companies—reportedly
Microsoft and SpaceX
—for roughly one-fifth of its revenue. Anthropic also reported an
$80.7B net loss
in the first six months of 2026, up from $42B in all of 2025, though the latest figure largely reflects accounting adjustments. Roughly $9B of the company's expenses comes from the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic has been using to train frontier models. Anthropic
warned
the models themselves could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," potentially exposing the company to lawsuits and regulations.
Investors appear to be treating the Anthropic IPO as a bellwether for AI confidence generally; the Nasdaq closed up 0.8% on yesterday’s news (S&P 500 +0.7%, Dow +0.3%). See Anthropic 101
here
Early Voting Shifts
More than 30 million Americans have voted in this year's midterms so far, with Election Day one week away. In Texas, over 4 million ballots have been cast, exceeding half of the state's 2022 turnout. The figures are from the University of Florida's Election Lab; see how your state compares
here
Voting methods are also shifting, particularly in parts of the South. In Georgia, roughly 95% of early votes have been cast in person, while mail ballot requests have
fallen more than 45%
from 2022. North Carolina has seen a similar split, recording 1.5 million in-person votes and about 60,000 mail ballots returned. Nationally, early votes are roughly even between in-person (15.4 million) and mail (15.1 million) as of this writing.
Experts say the shift may
reflect concerns
about mail ballots arriving on time or being counted, as well as a return to prepandemic voting habits. A Postal Service rule in effect since December largely postmarks mail when it's processed rather than dropped off, potentially pushing some ballots past deadlines.

Ancient Seafaring Amphibian
Scientists unearthed fossils of the first-known fully marine amphibian, according to a study published yesterday. The discovery could inform conservation efforts as freshwater salinization threatens amphibians.
Scroll here
for renderings and fossil images.
The two nearly complete skeletons found in southwestern China date to roughly 237 million years ago, when an ocean submerged the region. The amphibian, named Gerrothorax maritimus, was roughly between 2 and 3 feet long, with a disc-shaped body covered in bony armor. Experts believe this armor may have prevented water loss through its skin, allowing it to survive in saltwater. Modern amphibians, on the other hand, depend on their skin for respiration and water intake, making them dependent on freshwater habitats. Fewer than 2% of the more than 8,000 known species tolerate saltwater to any degree.
Researchers have recently found that
rising freshwater salt levels
—driven by mining, road deicers, and more—can reduce frogs' ability to fend off deadly diseases.
